answers.primary: A PostToolUse hook configured in the project's checked-in .claude/settings.json, matching the file-editing tools (Write, Edit, MultiEdit), which reads the edited path from the hook's JSON payload, filters for .ts/.tsx, and shells out to the formatter on exactly that file. The hook is a script in the repo so the behaviour travels with the checkout rather than living in prose.
answers.rejected_alternative: Leaving it as a CLAUDE.md / project-rules instruction, which is what is already in place and is exactly what fails: guidance is advisory and the model can drop it under context pressure.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness. The hook runner invokes the formatter unconditionally after a matching tool call, so compliance does not depend on the model remembering anything.
answers.context_boundary: The formatter runs in a separate OS process with no access to the conversation; only the hook's exit status and any stdout/stderr it emits are surfaced back into the agent's context window, so the token cost is a few lines rather than a formatting discussion.
answers.lifecycle: Fires after each successful matching tool call, for the whole session, on every developer who has the project settings loaded. It stops applying if the hook is removed from settings, if the matcher stops matching, or if the session never uses the built-in edit tools.
answers.failure_mode: It fails open on coverage rather than on execution: files rewritten through Bash (sed, a heredoc, a codegen script, git apply) never trigger a Write/Edit matcher and stay unformatted. It also creates a stale-content hazard because the formatter mutates the file after the model's last read, and if the formatter is missing or errors while the wrapper still exits zero, nothing surfaces. A CI formatting check remains the actual gate on what lands in a commit.
answers.version_caveat: Hook configuration lives in settings.json under a PostToolUse event with tool matchers, and the hook payload delivers the tool input as JSON on stdin. I cannot confirm from model knowledge alone the minimum Claude Code version that introduced this event or the exact payload field names for the edited path, so the script should read defensively and the version floor should be checked against the installed release.

answers.primary: Permission deny rules in the repo's checked-in .claude/settings.json, denying the read-capable tools against those paths (deny entries covering Read and Glob/Grep style access to ./.env, ./.env.*, and ./secrets/**), plus matching deny entries for the Bash surface so cat/less style reads are refused too.
answers.rejected_alternative: A PreToolUse hook that inspects each tool call's path argument and blocks it. That is more expressive but is extra code to maintain when the permission system already evaluates deny rules first.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness. The permission layer evaluates deny rules before the tool executes and the model never gets the file content, so this is not a matter of the model choosing to comply.
answers.context_boundary: Evaluation happens entirely in the harness before any tool result is produced; what crosses into the model's context is only a short refusal message naming the denied tool, never the file body.
answers.lifecycle: Applies from session start for anyone who opens the repo, because project settings are loaded with the project. It stops applying if the file is edited away, and it does not follow the secrets anywhere else on the machine.
answers.failure_mode: It fails closed for the built-in file tools but fails open around them: a Python or Node script the agent writes and runs reads the file directly, environment variables already exported into the shell leak the same values, and any path pattern the globs did not anticipate (.env.local, secrets nested under another directory, a symlink) slips through. Deny rules also cannot stop an MCP server or subprocess from reading the same bytes.
answers.version_caveat: Deny rules with per-tool specifiers such as Read(...) and Bash(...) are the mechanism, and deny takes precedence over allow. I cannot verify from model knowledge which release added file-read deny specifiers as distinct from Bash-only rules, nor the exact glob semantics for leading ./ versus bare patterns, so the rules must be tested against a real read attempt before being trusted.

answers.primary: A Notification hook in settings.json that runs a small OS-notifier command (PowerShell toast on Windows, terminal-notifier or osascript on macOS, notify-send on Linux) using the message and session details supplied on stdin. The command is the whole implementation; no model involvement at all.
answers.rejected_alternative: A Stop hook, which is the usual notify-me choice but fires when the turn ends rather than when the run is blocked mid-turn waiting on a person, so it answers a different question.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness. It decides when a notification event occurs and launches the command; the model neither knows nor influences whether an alert was raised.
answers.context_boundary: The notifier runs out of process and its output is not needed by the agent, so nothing meaningful crosses back into the context window. The blocked session stays parked exactly where it was.
answers.lifecycle: Triggered each time the CLI emits a notification event, which covers a pending permission prompt and a prolonged idle wait for input. It stops when the session ends or when the hook entry is removed.
answers.failure_mode: Purely advisory, and it fails silently open: if the notifier binary is absent, if the run is over SSH, inside a container, in WSL, or under a headless CI user, no toast appears and the run simply sits blocked with nobody informed. Notification storms during a chatty session also train people to ignore it.
answers.version_caveat: This depends on a Notification hook event existing in the installed version and on the idle-wait threshold that triggers it. I cannot confirm from model knowledge alone either the exact event name spelling or the idle timeout value, so both should be verified against the running release before promising the alert covers the input-wait case as well as the approval case.

answers.primary: An enterprise managed-settings policy file deployed by MDM to the system-level location (the ProgramData path on Windows, the equivalent system Application Support path on macOS, an /etc path on Linux), owned by root/Administrators and not writable by the developer, setting the permission policy that forbids the bypass-permissions mode and pins an acceptable default permission mode.
answers.rejected_alternative: Project-level .claude/settings.json committed to the repo, rejected because a developer can edit any repo they control and can simply run the agent from a different directory, so it cannot bind a fleet.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness, at the highest settings precedence tier. Managed policy overrides user and project settings by design, and the OS file ownership is what makes the override unliftable.
answers.context_boundary: Entirely outside every session's context window. The model never sees the policy; it only experiences the consequence, which is that approval prompts keep appearing.
answers.lifecycle: Read at process start for every session on that machine, so it applies to every run from the moment MDM lands the file, and it stops applying only when an administrator removes it or the machine drops out of management.
answers.failure_mode: Fails closed for the managed installation, but the boundary is the installation rather than the person: a developer with local admin rights, a second copy of the CLI installed under their own account, a container, a cloud dev box, or the Agent SDK used programmatically all sit outside this file. MDM drift detection and periodic re-application are what make the control real rather than one-time.
answers.version_caveat: This relies on managed/enterprise settings support and on a specific policy key that disables the bypass-permissions mode. I am reasonably confident such a key exists but I cannot verify its exact name or the minimum version from model knowledge alone, and enterprise-managed policy may be gated to Team/Enterprise plans, so both the key spelling and the plan requirement must be confirmed before the rollout is claimed to hold.

answers.primary: A Stop hook that checks for evidence that the suite ran and passed during this turn, and returns a blocking decision with a reason when it did not, sending the agent back to work. The evidence is produced deterministically by a companion PostToolUse hook that writes a per-session marker (test command, exit code, timestamp) whenever a test command actually executes, so the Stop hook verifies a fact rather than trusting a claim.
answers.rejected_alternative: A verification skill or a CLAUDE.md checklist telling the agent to run tests before declaring completion, rejected because the stated failure is the model forgetting, and advisory text cannot catch its own omission.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness owns the gate: it will not let the turn end while the hook blocks. The model owns only the remediation, which is to go run the tests.
answers.context_boundary: The hook executes outside the context window and reads state from disk. What crosses back in is the block reason string, which is injected as the continuation instruction, so the reason text should be short and directive.
answers.lifecycle: Fires whenever the main agent attempts to end its turn, and it stops blocking as soon as a passing run is recorded for that turn. The marker must be scoped and cleared per turn or the gate goes stale and starts passing on yesterday's green run.
answers.failure_mode: The characteristic failure is a loop: a hook that blocks unconditionally can pin the agent in a cycle, which is why the payload flag indicating the stop hook is already active must be honoured to break out. It fails open when the evidence check is naive, since running one trivial passing test satisfies a marker that only records that some test command ran. It also adds full-suite latency to every turn boundary, which pushes people to disable it.
answers.version_caveat: This depends on the Stop hook event supporting a structured blocking decision plus the re-entrancy flag in its payload, and on SubagentStop existing if the same rule must cover subagents. I cannot confirm the exact JSON field names or the minimum version from model knowledge alone. Note also that a user-initiated interrupt does not run the same path, so the gate does not cover an abandoned turn.

answers.primary: A PreToolUse hook matched on the Bash tool that parses the command string and, when it resolves to a push, returns a decision that forces a human confirmation (an ask decision where supported, otherwise a hard block whose reason tells the operator to perform the push themselves). Hooks run ahead of the tool regardless of the session's permission mode, which is what makes it survive the auto-approved configuration.
answers.rejected_alternative: An ask entry in the permissions block of settings.json for the push pattern, rejected because the permission-mode configuration is exactly what has been turned off for speed, so a rule evaluated by that same layer is not guaranteed to survive it.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness. The hook decides before the command runs and the model cannot talk its way past a returned deny.
answers.context_boundary: Matching runs in a separate process that sees only the tool input JSON. The decision and its reason string are what cross back into the model's context; the confirmation itself happens in the operator's terminal, outside the model's view.
answers.lifecycle: Evaluated on every Bash tool call for the life of the session, and it stops applying if the hook entry is removed or if the push is performed through a surface that is not the Bash tool, such as an MCP git server.
answers.failure_mode: String matching on a shell command is the weak point and it fails open under paraphrase: git -C elsewhere push, a push hidden behind an alias, a wrapper script, a compound command joined with && or ;, or a push triggered by a hook inside the repo all miss a naive pattern. It fails closed only if the matcher treats anything it cannot fully parse as a push candidate. In a headless or non-interactive run there is no human to confirm, so the safe behaviour there is outright denial rather than an indefinite wait.
answers.version_caveat: The ask-style permission decision returned from a PreToolUse hook is the cleanest shape, but I cannot verify from model knowledge alone whether an ask decision is still honoured when the session is running with permission prompting bypassed. Until that is tested on the installed version, implement the rule as an explicit deny with an instructive reason, which is unambiguous in every mode.

answers.primary: A PreToolUse hook on the Bash tool that appends the full command string, timestamp, session id, user and working directory to an append-only audit sink, paired with a PostToolUse hook on the same tool that records the outcome so the record distinguishes attempted from executed. It is deployed through managed settings so developers do not opt out, and it writes to a location the developer cannot rewrite (a syslog/SIEM forwarder rather than a file in their home directory).
answers.rejected_alternative: Reconstructing the record from session transcripts after the fact, rejected because transcripts are local, user-modifiable, and describe what was said as much as what ran.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness. The hook receives the actual tool input the harness is about to execute, so the record does not depend on the model reporting honestly.
answers.context_boundary: Logging happens in a separate process on the tool payload, and it returns nothing to the agent, so the audit trail costs no context and the model has no view of what was recorded.
answers.lifecycle: Fires on every Bash tool invocation while the managed configuration is in force. It stops covering anything the moment work moves to a machine or an install that does not load the policy.
answers.failure_mode: Fails open by design, since a logging hook that errors should not stop the developer, which means a broken forwarder produces silence rather than an alarm; the sink therefore needs its own heartbeat. Coverage is also narrower than the compliance ask sounds: it captures the command the agent submitted, not what a spawned shell, a build script, an interactive process, or an MCP server subsequently executed, and a locally written log file is tamperable.
answers.version_caveat: This depends on the hook payload exposing the command verbatim under a stable field for the Bash tool, and on managed settings being able to define hooks that project and user settings cannot override. I cannot confirm either the field name or the override precedence for hooks from model knowledge alone. There may also be a first-party telemetry/OTel export that satisfies this more cleanly, possibly plan-gated, which should be checked before building custom logging.

answers.primary: A PreToolUse hook on the Bash tool implementing an explicit allowlist: parse the command, and if it is a single simple command that is exactly the approved read-only invocation with no shell metacharacters, return an allow decision so it runs without prompting; if it is any other aws invocation, or anything the parser cannot fully resolve, return deny.
answers.rejected_alternative: Expressing it purely as settings.json permission rules, an allow entry for the one command plus a deny entry covering the aws prefix. This is rejected because deny is evaluated ahead of allow, so a blanket aws deny also kills the one command that is supposed to pass, and enumerating every other aws subcommand as a deny is not exhaustive.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness. The hook decision is applied before execution and the allow path is what removes the prompt, so neither the block nor the exemption depends on the model.
answers.context_boundary: Parsing runs out of process on the tool input string. Only the decision and a short reason cross back, which is also how the agent learns to stop trying other aws commands.
answers.lifecycle: Evaluated on every Bash call for the whole session, and it lapses if the hook is unregistered or if aws is reached some other way, for example through a Python boto3 script or an MCP server that wraps the same API.
answers.failure_mode: Command-string allowlisting fails open against composition unless it is written paranoid: a semicolon or && chain, an env prefix, an absolute path to the binary, quoting tricks, aws with a profile flag, or the command passed through sh -c all evade a naive equality check. Default-deny on anything unparsed is what turns this into a fail-closed control. Conversely an over-strict matcher rejects the legitimate call with extra flags and the team routes around the hook.
answers.version_caveat: The important semantics here are the prefix-matching grammar for Bash permission specifiers and the deny-over-allow precedence, plus the ability of a PreToolUse hook to return an allow decision that suppresses the prompt. I cannot verify the exact matcher grammar or that allow-from-hook fully bypasses prompting on the installed version from model knowledge alone, so both need a live test.

answers.primary: This is not a Claude Code extension problem at all: it needs OS-level isolation. Launch the whole agent inside a sandbox or container whose filesystem view simply does not contain those paths, either the harness's own OS sandbox mechanism (Seatbelt on macOS, bubblewrap/Landlock style confinement on Linux) or a devcontainer with the credential paths not mounted. Kernel-enforced confinement is inherited by every descendant process, which is the property that path-based tool blocks lack.
answers.rejected_alternative: A PreToolUse hook or additional permission deny rules covering more tools, rejected because it is the same class of control that has already been shown to stop only the agent's own tool calls and not a child process opening the file directly.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness and ultimately the kernel. Once the process tree is confined, the read fails with a permission error no matter which program in the tree attempts it.
answers.context_boundary: The confinement wraps the entire agent process and everything it spawns, so it sits underneath the context window entirely. The only thing that reaches the model is an ordinary access-denied error from whatever tool it ran.
answers.lifecycle: Applied at launch and in force for the life of the process tree, including children of children. It stops applying the instant someone starts the agent outside the wrapper, which is why the launcher, not the settings file, is the thing that must be controlled.
answers.failure_mode: Fails closed, which is the point, but it breaks legitimate work: anything that genuinely needs AWS or SSH credentials now fails, and the pressure to punch a hole in the sandbox is the real risk. Coverage gaps remain where a helper daemon, an agent-forwarding socket, or a network service outside the sandbox can be asked to use the credentials on the agent's behalf, and the sandbox story is materially weaker on Windows, where a container is usually the only honest answer.
answers.version_caveat: Native sandboxing in the CLI is a comparatively recent and platform-limited capability, and I cannot confirm from model knowledge alone the setting name, the supported platforms, or the minimum version in the installed release. If native sandboxing is unavailable or experimental there, a container with an explicit mount list is the version-independent implementation.

answers.primary: An enterprise managed-settings policy file deployed by MDM at the system path and owned by an administrator, which both ships the approved extensions (ideally as a single IT-controlled plugin from an IT-controlled marketplace, bundling the hooks, skills, subagents and MCP server definitions) and disables discovery of the user-level and project-level equivalents, including the flags that would otherwise let a repo's own MCP server definitions be enabled.
answers.rejected_alternative: Distributing a blessed .claude directory into every repo as the source of truth, rejected because project-level configuration is exactly what a developer can edit or add to, so it cannot be the thing that decides what is allowed to load.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness at the top settings precedence tier, backed by OS file ownership so the policy itself cannot be edited locally. The model has no say in which extensions exist.
answers.context_boundary: The policy is evaluated at session startup, outside any context window. What the model sees is simply a narrower menu: the approved skills, subagents and tools appear and nothing else does.
answers.lifecycle: Read at the start of every session on a managed machine and re-applied by MDM on drift. It stops governing anything launched from an unmanaged install, a container image the developer built, or the Agent SDK used directly.
answers.failure_mode: Fails closed for the extension surfaces the policy actually enumerates, and fails open for any surface it does not. That is the durable weakness: each new extension type added to the product defaults to loading until the policy is updated, so this control needs review at every upgrade. It also does not stop behavioural influence, since repo files and CLAUDE.md text still steer the agent even when no developer-authored code loads.
answers.version_caveat: I am confident managed settings exist and can constrain MCP server loading (including a project-MCP enable flag and a disallowed-servers list), but I cannot verify from model knowledge alone that current managed settings expose keys to suppress user-level and project-level hooks, skills and subagent definitions, nor the plugin-marketplace pinning keys or their plan gating. The full guarantee as stated should be treated as unproven until the available managed keys are enumerated against the installed version.
